name: Skíðblaðnir
powers: Folds up like a cloth into a pocket; always has a fair wind.
description: The best of all ships, built for Freyr by the dwarven sons of Ivaldi. Large enough to carry all the gods and their weapons, yet it can be folded like a cloth and carried in a pouch when not at sea. It always finds a fair wind wherever it sails. In the Prose Edda, Skíðblaðnir is listed among the treasures the dwarves made for the gods.

name: The Sunken Church Bell
powers: Said to ring from beneath the water on holy nights, and to be recoverable only by one pure of heart.
description: A recurring Swedish folk motif: a church bell lost in a lake — swept overboard while being ferried, or dragged down by the water folk (or a troll) because its ringing disturbed them. The bell is said to toll faintly beneath the surface on Christmas night or other holy nights, and treasure-hunters who try to raise it with a pure heart may catch a glimpse of it before it slips away. Variants are told across Sweden, Norway, and Finland.

name: Sampo
powers: Grinds out grain, salt, and gold for its possessor.
description: The wonder-working mill of Finnish epic, forged by the smith Ilmarinen as the price for the hand of the maiden of Pohjola. The Sampo ground out limitless grain, salt, and gold, making its possessor rich. In the Kalevala, the heroes of Väinölä and the mistress of Pohjola fight over it; in the battle the Sampo is smashed and lost at sea, and its fragments grant the sea its richness. Its shape and true nature are never fully described.

name: Sif's Golden Hair
aliases: The Gold of the Sons of Ivaldi
powers: Grows from the head like real hair and never loses its gleam.
description: The golden hair of Sif, wife of Thor, wrought by the dwarven sons of Ivaldi after Loki maliciously cut off her own. Made of gold so fine that it grew from her head like real hair, it became proof of the dwarves' skill and opened the great contest of gifts between rival smiths. Loki commissioned it to atone for his mischief, and Thor kept his skull intact.

name: Svalinn
powers: Tempering the sun's rays so the earth and sea are not consumed by fire.
description: The shield that stands before the sun, named in Grímnismál, sheltering earth and sea from the burning rays of the sun goddess Sól. The poem warns that if the shield ever falls away, mountains and the deep sea would be consumed by flame. It is one of the most purely cosmic objects in the Eddic corpus, a world-sustaining object rather than a warrior's arm.

name: Smjörstafur
powers: Brings success in making butter.
description: Smjörstafur, the butter stave of the Huld manuscript, drawn or carved to bring success in butter-making. In an agrarian world where dairy was wealth, a charm for a full churn was practical magic, and the stave sits among the agricultural signs recorded beside the luck and protection staves of the grimoires.

name: The Völva's Staff
material: Wood with a metal knob (per saga description)
powers: The badge of the völva's office, used in the working of seidr and prophecy.
description: The staff of the seeress or völva, who in saga accounts carried a knobbed staff as the badge of her office. Eiríks saga rauða describes the seeress Þorbjörg with a staff topped with a brass knob as she worked her seidr. Iron rods found in Viking-age female graves may be such staffs, though the identification is debated by archaeologists.

name: The Sun Chariot
powers: Carries the sun across the sky until the wolf Sköll swallows it at Ragnarök.
description: The chariot of Sól, the sun goddess, drawn across the sky by the horses Arvakr and Alsvinn, with the shield Svalinn before them to temper the light. The wolves Sköll and Hati hunt the sun and moon, and at Ragnarök Sköll will at last swallow the sun. The chariot is described in Grímnismál and Gylfaginning.

name: Signbook
powers: Formulas and signs for 'signing' wounds, bleeding, illness, and fire.
description: A signbook (signeringsbok), a hand-copied Swedish book of signs used by folk healers and 'kloka gummor', the wise women and men of the parish. The volumes collected prayers, magical signs, and formulae for 'signing' wounds, bleeding, disease, and fire. Several Swedish signbooks from the 17th to 19th centuries survive in archives, mixing Christian prayers with folk-magical practice.
source: Swedish folk-medicine collections (e.g. Nordiska museet, Riksarkivet)

name: Silver Buckles
description: Silver buckles and clasps worn with Swedish regional folk dress, on belts, shoes, and collars. Such silver, often inherited and re-used across generations, was engraved with initials and dates and served as both ornament and stored wealth. Wealthy folk wore heavy rectangular 'spännen'; poorer folk wore simpler clasps. The buckles are a documented part of the folk-costume tradition.

name: The Skin Satchel
maker: Sewn for a magical purpose in the tale
powers: Holds an impossible store or releases the tale's marvels.
description: A satchel made of animal skin that carries magic in a Swedish folk tale. In the tale 'The Skin Satchel', the humble leather bag turns out to hold an impossible store, or to have been sewn for a magical purpose, and its opening releases the story's marvels. The satchel is one of many everyday objects in Swedish wonder-tales that conceal power.

name: The Silver Spoon
maker: Said to be left by the vittra
powers: A sign of the hidden people's favour.
description: A silver spoon said to be left by the vittra, the hidden folk of northern Sweden, for humans who helped them or as a sign of favour. In folk tradition such a spoon appeared where none had been, or a borrowed spoon returned with a gift of silver. The spoon is a token of the hidden people's goodwill and a typical vittra gift.
source: Northern Swedish tradition of the vittra

name: The Sea King's Ring
maker: Given by the sea king in the ballad
powers: Binds the maiden to the sea king.
description: A golden ring given by the sea king in the Swedish ballad 'Agneta and the Sea King', a version of the old ballad about the maiden taken by the sea folk. The ring is the gift that binds the maiden to her underwater master; in the ballad's ending the ring and its owner part in sorrow. The ballad is documented in Swedish song collections from the 18th century.
source: Swedish ballad 'Agneta and the Sea King'

name: Stavkirke
description: A medieval Norwegian timber church built on a post-and-plank frame, with steep shingled roofs, carved portals, and dragon-head finials. Around thirty stave churches survive of the more than a thousand once built, among them Borgund, Urnes, and Heddal. In folklore the churches mark where the old faith met the new, and legends tell of trolls turned to stone at the sound of their bells.

name: Sámi Drum
powers: Used by the noaidi, the Sámi shaman, to see hidden things, find lost reindeer, and answer questions.
description: The frame drum of the Sámi shaman, or noaidi, a shallow bowl of carved pine covered with reindeer skin painted in red alder juice with figures of gods, animals, and the sun. Struck with a reindeer-horn hammer while the noaidi sang, the drum revealed answers in the path of a jumping ring. Hundreds were burned by missionaries in the 18th century, and survivors are treasured museum objects.

name: Sieidi Stone
powers: An offering stone believed to grant luck in hunting, fishing, and reindeer herding to those who sacrifice.
description: A natural stone, boulder, or outcrop venerated by the Sámi as the dwelling of a spirit and a place of offering, the sieidi or seita. Hunters, fishers, and herders left antlers, bones, silver, or food at sieidis to secure luck and damaged the stone when crossed. Many stand at lakes, rivers, and passes across Norwegian Sápmi, and the custom survived in the far north into modern times.

name: Stabbur
material: Timber raised on stone or wooden pillars
description: The Norwegian timber storehouse raised off the ground on wooden posts or stones to keep food and valuables safe from damp and vermin. Stabburs held grain, meat, wool, and heirlooms, and the loft door was reached by an outside stair. Protection mattered in folk belief as much as locks, and protective marks were sometimes cut into doorways, as surviving forest-finn barns show.

name: Sølje
description: A Norwegian silver brooch worn at the throat, made of a central disc with dangling pendants and fine wirework. Søljer were the most important piece of a woman's festive dress, passed down in families, and often given as betrothal gifts. Regional workshops shaped local variants, and the brooch remains part of the bunad worn at weddings and on Constitution Day.

name: The Snow Queen's Mirror
powers: Reflects everything good and fair as mean and ugly; splinters pierce the heart and eye.
description: The devil's magic mirror from the first chapter of Andersen's 'The Snow Queen'. It magnifies everything ugly and shrinks all that is good, and when the trolls drop it, it shatters into millions of splinters. Splinters blown into the eyes and hearts of the children Kay and Gerda set the story in motion, for Kay's changed vision is what lets the Snow Queen take him away.

name: The Steadfast Tin Soldier
material: Tin, cast from an old tin spoon
powers: Falls from the window, rides a paper boat, and is swallowed by a fish, yet never bends.
description: The one-legged toy soldier of Andersen's tale, cast last from the family's old tin spoon and brave out of all proportion. Sailing his paper boat through the gutter and burned at last in the stove with the paper dancer he loved, he never flinches. The tale made the plain tin soldier a figure of quiet constancy and one of Andersen's most loved objects.
source: Hans Christian Andersen, Den standhaftige tinsoldat (1838)

name: Sibylline Books
powers: Prophetic verses consulted by the Roman state to avert calamities; their burning punished Tarquin's haggling.
description: The nine books of prophetic verses the Cumaean Sibyl offered to Tarquinius Superbus, of which she burned six and sold the last three at the original price, as Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus relate; kept in the temple of Jupiter, the surviving Sibylline Books were consulted for Rome's most dangerous crises.
source: Livy, History of Rome; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Roman Antiquities

name: Sword of Damocles
maker: Hung at the court of Dionysius II of Syracuse
powers: Showed Damocles the peril hidden in royal ease; the emblem of insecurity in power.
description: The sword suspended by a single horse-hair over the head of Damocles, courtier of Dionysius II of Syracuse, to show him the insecurity of royal power; when Damocles envied the tyrant's life, Dionysius made him taste it, and the hanging sword became the emblem of peril in high office. Told by Cicero in the Tusculan Disputations.

name: Santo Caliz
material: Agate cup with gold mounts, pearls, and gems
era: Agate cup of the 2nd-1st century BC; mounts medieval
maker: Unknown Hellenistic or Roman lapidary; goldwork by later craftsmen
powers: Venerated as the cup of the Last Supper; its identification is tradition, not verified history.
description: The Holy Chalice of Valencia, an agate cup of the 2nd-1st century BC set in medieval gold mounts, kept in Valencia Cathedral since 1437; tradition identifies it as the cup of the Last Supper, brought from Jerusalem via Rome and Huesca, but that identification cannot be verified and is disputed. The cup itself is genuine and ancient.
source: Valencia Cathedral tradition; A. Beltran, archaeological study (1960)

name: Scarab Amulet
powers: Protection against evil; associated with rebirth.
description: A scarab-shaped amulet crafted from glazed faience, representing the beetle god Khepri who rolls the sun across the sky. Such amulets were placed in burials to ensure safe passage and rebirth in the afterlife.

name: Scepter of Ra
powers: Authority of the sun god; used in prayers and royal ceremonies.
description: The Was scepter, a long staff with a forked tip, was the emblem of power and dominion of the sun god Ra. It appears in temple reliefs and on royal crowns, symbolizing the pharaoh's role as the earthly representative of Ra.

name: Gáe Assail
powers: Unstoppable spear of the champion of the Tuatha Dé Danann.
description: Gáe Assail, the great spear of Lugh, one of the four treasures the Tuatha Dé Danann carried into Ireland. Lugh used it at the Second Battle of Mag Tuired, where it helped rout the Fomorians. Its name preserves an older association with the Otherworld gift-bearers of Irish tradition.

name: Szczerbiec
powers: Symbol of Polish kingship; the notched blade carries the Kiev legend.
description: Szczerbiec, the jagged sword used at Polish coronations from the Middle Ages. Its name, 'the notched one', recalls the legend that Bolesław the Brave struck it against the Golden Gate of Kiev in 1018. The surviving blade, now in Wawel Castle, was damaged in a nineteenth-century theft.

name: Great Torc of Snettisham
description: The Great Torc of Snettisham, a necklace of two interlocking gold-alloy rings with ornate buffer terminals, made in eastern England around 75 BC and found in a hoard at Snettisham, Norfolk, in 1950. Such tores marked high status among Iron Age Britons; the example is a centrepiece of the British Museum's Celtic collection.

name: Selkie's Seal-Skin
powers: Lets the selkie shed human form and return to the sea when put back on.
description: The seal-skin of the selkie, the shapeshifting seal-people of Scottish and Irish tradition. A selkie sheds the skin to take human form on land and must have it returned to go back to the sea; a human who hides the skin keeps the selkie as a spouse until the skin is found. The motif underpins the classic selkie-bride tales.

name: Silver Branch of Emain
powers: Its music lulled listeners and summoned heroes to the Otherworld.
description: The silver apple-branch carried by a woman of the Otherworld to the hero Bran in the medieval tale the Voyage of Bran. Its music lulls those who hear it, and Bran leaves with its bearer for the Land of Women across the sea. Messengers of the Irish Otherworld traditionally bear such singing branches.

name: The Magic Mirror
powers: Told its owner who was the fairest in the land.
description: The magic mirror of the queen in the Grimm tale of Snow White. Each time she asks 'Mirror, mirror on the wall, who is the fairest of them all?', the mirror answers truly, and its answer drives the queen to send Snow White into the wood. The mirror is a test-object of the tale and exists only in fiction.

name: The Six Swans' Shirts
powers: Thrown over her swan brothers, restored them to human form.
description: The six shirts of stinging nettles woven in silence by the sister in the Grimms' tale of the six swans. For years she must sew them without speaking a word; when at last they are thrown over her brothers, the swans become men again. The shirt-making is the tale's central task and ordeal.

name: The Scales of Ma'at
powers: Weighs the heart of the dead against the feather of truth in the judgment hall.
description: The great balance set up in the Hall of Two Truths, where the heart of the dead was weighed against the feather of Ma'at before Osiris, with Thoth recording the result. Chapter 125 of the Book of the Dead describes the rite, while the devourer Ammit waits to swallow any heart found heavier than the feather. The scene is among the most reproduced images of Egyptian religion.

name: The Sistrum
powers: Its rattling pleased the goddess and drove away hostile powers.
description: A sacred rattle of looped bronze rods strung across a frame, shaken in the cult of Hathor and Isis to please the goddess and repel evil with its hissing sound. Priestesses, queens, and kings bore it in temple ritual, and great ceremonial versions stood as temple furniture. Its naos-shaped variant carried the cow-eared head of Hathor between its handles and remained in use into Graeco-Roman Egypt.

name: The Solar Barque of Ra
powers: Carries the sun across the sky by day and through the underworld by night.
description: The two celestial boats in which the sun god Ra sails: the day barque Mandjet crossing the sky and the night barque Mesektet crossing the Duat, where the crew repels the serpent Apep with spears. The nightly battle myth inspired real solar barques buried beside temples and pyramids, including the Khufu boat, so that the king might make the same journey after death.
source: Pyramid Texts and solar barque burials

name: The Senet Board
powers: Its play mirrored the soul's passage through the hazards of the afterlife.
description: The Egyptian board game of thirty squares in three rows, played with counters and knucklebones, the most common game board found in Egypt. The crossing of its hazardous squares mirrored the soul's journey through the afterlife, and the Book of the Dead shows the deceased playing senet against an invisible opponent to win passage. Complete boards, including Tutankhamun's, survive from royal tombs.
source: Excavated boards; Book of the Dead vignettes

name: The Feather of the Simurgh
powers: Burned as a signal, its smoke summons the great bird to help.
description: The feather given by the great bird Simurgh to the hero Zal and later to his son Rostam, to be burned whenever they needed the bird's aid, at whose smoke Simurgh came flying. In the Shahnameh the feather carries the abandoned boy Zal to safety and later rescues Rostam in his direst need. In later Sufi poetry it became an emblem of the soul's reliance on divine help.

name: The Seal of Solomon
material: Gold ring set with a stone (mythic)
powers: By its engraving of the divine Name, its bearer commanded the winds, beasts, and jinn.
description: The signet ring of the prophet-king Solomon, engraved with the divine Name, by whose power he commanded the winds, beasts, and jinn in Jewish and Islamic tradition alike, told in the Quran, the midrash, and the Thousand and One Nights. Its seal, often drawn as a six-pointed star, later became a widespread protective emblem across the Middle East, North Africa, and Europe.
source: Quran; midrash; Thousand and One Nights

name: Solomon's Flying Carpet
powers: Carried the king, his throne, and his court through the air on the wind.
description: The carpet of Solomon, woven of silk and green stuff, said in Islamic tradition to be large enough to bear the king, his throne, and his whole court, carried through the air by the wind at his command and shaded by a flock of birds overhead. The Quran records the wind as made subject to Solomon, and later commentators expanded this into the famous flying carpet, whose details grow in the tellings.
source: Quran; al-Tabari; al-Kisa'i; Thousand and One Nights

name: Sefer Yetzirah
maker: Tradition attributes it to the patriarch Abraham
powers: Describes the creation of the world through the Hebrew letters and the ten sefirot.
description: The earliest surviving Hebrew text of Jewish mysticism, the 'Book of Formation,' which describes how the world was created through the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet and the ten sefirot, and sets out paths by which the mystic may emulate that act. Its opening lines attribute it to the patriarch Abraham, and it shaped the whole later development of Kabbalah.

name: The Sword of Goliath
powers: The heavy blade of the Philistine champion, kept as a relic at Nob.
description: The sword of the Philistine champion Goliath, taken as spoil after David slew him and later kept wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod at the sanctuary of Nob, where the fugitive David received it, saying there was none like it. The weapon is described in the First Book of Samuel, and David's possession of it anchors his kingship narrative in the biblical account.

name: The Sword of Antar
powers: The great blade of the warrior-poet, wielded in his duels and tribal wars.
description: The sword Dhami, the chosen blade of Antarah ibn Shaddad, the pre-Islamic warrior-poet of the Arabian Peninsula whose exploits fill the medieval romance Sirah 'Antar. In the sira, Antar wins the sword in combat and carries it through the wars of the tribe of Abs and his long struggle to marry Abla. The romance is literary, and the sword's named exploits grow with the telling.

name: Shichishito
powers: None (honorific and ritual sword)
description: An iron sword with seven branch-like projections along the blade, dedicated to the Isonokami Shrine and recorded in the Nihon Shoki as a gift from the kingdom of Baekje. Its long inlaid inscription describing offerings to the sun deity makes it a rare physical relic of early Korean-Japanese exchange and a treasure of Japanese shrine keeping.

name: Shimenawa
powers: Marks off divine ground and repels impurity
description: A sacred rope twisted from rice straw and hung before shrines, torii gates, and sacred trees to mark off divine ground. Its origin is tied to the rope strung across the cave mouth after Amaterasu emerged, preventing the sun goddess from retreating; the shimenawa now seals off the kami's dwelling places from impurity.

name: Sweetgrass Basket
era: From the colonial era to the present
powers: Carries the memory of African weaving in every coil.
description: Coiled baskets woven from sweetgrass and palmetto leaf by Gullah weavers of the Lowcountry, a craft brought to America from West Africa and continued on the rice coast for three centuries. The tight coil stitch is nearly unchanged from African prototypes, and the baskets long served in rice processing before becoming prized art. The tradition survives in Mount Pleasant and the Sea Islands.
source: Gullah weaving tradition and cultural studies

name: Saci's Red Cap
aliases: The Cap of the One-Legged Imp
era: Brazilian folk tradition to the present
powers: Whoever wins it gains the Saci's power.
description: The red knitted cap worn by Saci, the one-legged mischief spirit of Brazilian folklore; to take it is to gain Saci's obedience or his magic, and tales tell of those who steal it only to lose it again. Saci is said to rest his spinning tricks and whistling when he sleeps, the cap beside him. The cap alone identifies him in folk art and story.
source: Brazilian oral tradition and Monteiro Lobato's tales

name: Supay Figurine
powers: Opens the door to the world beneath the earth.
description: Images and masks of Supay, the lord of the Andean underworld known as uku pacha, the world beneath the earth, honored and feared for his rule over the dead and the mountain's depths. In the colonial era his name was pressed into service for the devil, and festivals still carry the blurred figure, half ancient lord, half devil. His power is invoked at carnival and in the mines.
source: Andean oral tradition and colonial records

name: The Golden Stool (Sika Dwa)
powers: Holds the soul (sunsum) of the Asante nation; its wellbeing is the nation's wellbeing.
description: The Sika Dwa, or Golden Stool, is the sacred stool of the Asante, a gold-covered stool kept unseated-on as the soul (sunsum) of the nation. Tradition holds that Okomfo Anokye called it down from heaven in the 1700s, settling it onto the lap of Osei Tutu. It may not touch the ground and remains the supreme emblem of Asante sovereignty.
source: Asante oral tradition; Manhyia Palace Museum

name: Sabar Drum
description: The sabar is the lead drum of Wolof and Serer music of Senegal, a single-headed drum played with one hand and a curved stick. Played at ceremonies and wrestling matches, its rhythms are named and can 'talk', and master drummers lead communal dance. Sabar ensembles anchor celebration and social life across Senegal.

name: Sao Bronze Bracelet
description: Bronze and copper ornaments cast by the Sao people of the Lake Chad basin, an urban civilisation that flourished in what is now Chad for over a millennium. Excavated bracelets, anklets, and figurines from Sao mound sites show accomplished lost-wax casting; major finds are kept at the National Museum of N'Djamena and studied as key evidence of ancient Central African metalwork.
source: Sao archaeological finds; National Museum of N'Djamena

name: Somali Dabqaad Incense Burner
description: The dabqaad is a clay or soapstone incense burner of Somalia, its bowl raised on short legs and covered by a perforated lid from which smoke rises. Frankincense and myrrh smoulder in it at home to perfume rooms and welcome guests, keeping alive the incense tradition of the Horn of Africa.

name: Sudanese Kaskara Sword
description: The kaskara is a straight, double-edged sword with a plain iron cross-guard and disc pommel, carried in Sudan and adjacent regions into the 20th century. It descends from medieval Arab forms and served as a fighting blade and ceremonial weapon; many bear inscriptions, marks, or leather-wrapped grips, and were worn as signs of honour.

name: Sudanese Girba Water-Skin
description: The girba is a water vessel of Sudan made from a whole tanned animal hide, treated to be watertight, with openings at the neck and legs. Carried by travellers and herders across the Sahel and Nubia, it keeps water cool through evaporation; its shape and use are documented in travel accounts of the Nile lands.
source: Travel accounts of the Nile lands; museum collections

name: Sudarshana Chakra
description: Whirling discus carried by Vishnu, the Sudarshana Chakra, described in the Puranas as a blazing thousand-spoked weapon that flies to its target and returns to its master. It appears in Vishnu's upper right hand beside the conch, lotus and mace, and is hurled in avatar legends, such as the slaying of the demons Jay and Vijay, against foes who cannot be defeated by other means.

name: Shiva Lingam
description: Aniconic emblem of Shiva worshipped as a polished stone or carved shaft rising from a yoni base, standing for the god's infinite and formless power. Lingams are anointed daily with water, milk and bilva leaves across India, and the Puranas hold that Shiva once appeared as a column of fire whose ends neither Brahma nor Vishnu could find, a legend re-enacted in the lingam's worship.

name: Sankha Conch
description: Right-whorled conch shell blown at Hindu ceremonies and held by Vishnu as Panchajanya, the war-conch of the god. In the Puranas Vishnu sounds the conch before battle, and the sankha is still blown to open worship and marriage rites, its deep note believed to dispel inauspicious forces and to mark the boundary of sacred space.
source: Vishnu Purana; Hindu temple and marriage ritual

name: Sacred Tooth Relic
description: Relic of a tooth of the Buddha enshrined in the Temple of the Sacred Tooth in Kandy, the most venerated Buddhist object in Sri Lanka. According to the Mahavamsa the tooth was smuggled to the island from India and carried by successive rulers, and annual perahera processions honour it as guardian of the land and of its kings.
era: according to tradition, 4th century AD onwards
maker: enshrined by Sinhalese kings; reliquaries by court goldsmiths
source: Mahavamsa and the chronicle of the Tooth Relic (Dalada-vamsa)

name: Sanni Yaksha Mask
description: Carved wooden mask of a Sinhalese disease demon, one of the eighteen sanni masks painted in vivid colours and worn in exorcism ceremonies. Each mask portrays a specific affliction such as fever, madness or jaundice, and the dance of the mask is performed to trick the demon and dismiss it from the sick body, a practice known as tovil.
source: Sinhalese ritual ethnography and mask-carving tradition

name: Sindhi Topi
description: Embroidered cylindrical cap of Sindh, worn by men and at festivals, with a band of stitched mirror-work and a rounded crown. The sindhi topi is a national symbol of the province, worn with the ajrak shawl, and Sindhi folklore holds that the cap carries the honour and pride of the wearer, so that to knock it off is a grave insult.

name: Singing Bowl
description: Metal bowl that rings a sustained tone when its rim is rubbed with a wooden striker, used in Himalayan Buddhist ritual for offerings and meditation. The bowls are held to clear and focus the mind, and their sound is used to open and close ceremonies in the monasteries of Nepal and Tibet, where the ringing is read as an offering to the deities.
source: Himalayan ritual practice and craft tradition

name: Sherpa Pangden
description: Striped front apron woven and worn by Sherpa married women over their chuba, the pangden's narrow red, white and black stripes marking the wearer's married status. The aprons are woven on backstrap looms from sheep and yak wool, and Sherpa tradition regards them as a badge of the household and of womanhood, also woven in neighbouring Tibet.
source: Sherpa weaving and dress ethnography (Dolma Sherpa)

name: Solomon Islands Shell Money
description: Traditional currency of the Solomon Islands, made from small discs ground from shell and strung on fibre in long coils. Shell money is still used in bride-price, compensation and chiefly exchange, its value fixed by the species of shell and the skill of its making, and the red feather-money of the Reef Islands is among the most prized forms.
source: Ethnographic studies of Solomon Islands economy

name: Samoan Siapo (Tapa)
description: Barkcloth of Samoa, beaten from the inner bark of the paper mulberry into large sheets and painted or printed with geometric patterns in earth tones. Siapo is made by women for wrapping, dress and ceremony, and its designs are handed down within families, each district owning particular patterns that mark the cloth as its own.
source: Ethnographic records of Samoan material culture

name: Samoan ʻIe Toga (Fine Mat)
description: Treasured fine mat of Samoa, woven from the thinnest strips of pandanus by senior women and polished with oil to a fine sheen. The ʻie toga is the highest form of Samoan wealth, exchanged at weddings, funerals and political occasions, and the oldest mats are given names and genealogies and counted among the most sacred possessions of the family.
source: Ethnographic scholarship on Samoan ceremonial exchange

name: Samoan Tātau Tools
description: Set of combs and mallets used in the Samoan tatau, the traditional hand-tapped tattoo applied by a tufuga ta tatau. A comb of bone or turtle shell set with teeth is dipped in soot pigment and struck with a wooden mallet to drive ink into the skin, a practice preserved by legend from the goddesses Taema and Tilafaiga, who brought the art from Fiti.
material: bone, turtle shell, wood, soot pigment
source: Ethnographic accounts of Samoan tattooing; oral tradition

name: Sakta Brooch
description: The sakta, the ancient Baltic breast brooch of bronze, silver or silver-gilt, fastened the folk costume — especially the bride's — at throat or chest. Archaeological finds date the fibula type back two millennia; the later 'bubble' saktas with hemispherical bosses and glass eyes were trusted as savings. A Latvian folk song says goddess Laima makes fibulae for a girl, 'immersing them in silver'.
source: Latvijas Banka, Gold Brooches: The Bubble Fibula; Latvian archaeological and ethnographic collections

name: Seto Folk Costume
description: The Seto women's folk costume of south-eastern Estonia's Setomaa: a striking white, black and red ensemble of striped or checked skirt, linen blouse, woven belt and silver jewellery, worn for leelo singing, church feasts and Seto Kingdom Day. The costume is integral to the Seto polyphonic leelo tradition inscribed by UNESCO in 2009, in which choirs sang in traditional dress.
source: UNESCO: Seto Leelo, Seto polyphonic singing tradition (2009); Visit Setomaa ethnographic accounts
